case_name: University Of Kerala v Council, Principals', Colleges, Kerala & Others
facts: The Council of Principals of Colleges in Kerala filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging various universities in the State of Kerala had issued directions by way of letters/circulars to conduct election to the colleges' unions.
The main challenge was that the impugned circulars/letters had no statutory basis, and hence were invalid.

The Kerala High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed those letters/circulars directing following the presidential system of election in the students' union election and left it free to the colleges to follow the system of their choice.
issues: Whether after getting the recommendations of some expert body by a court order, the Court itself can implement the said recommendations by passing a judicial order or whether the Court can only send it to the Legislature or its delegate to consider making a law for implementation of these recommendations
Whether the judiciary should seek to perform legislative or executive functions
petitioner_arguments: The impugned circulars/letters had no statutory basis, and hence were invalid.
The Court should not encroach into the sphere of the other organs of the State.
court_reasoning: Judicial powers is not immune against this human weakness. It also must be on guard against encroaching beyond its proper bounds, and not the less so since the only restraint upon it is self-restraint.

The Court should have thereafter, instead of passing a judicial order directing implementation of the recommendations, sent it to the appropriate Legislature or its delegate (which in this case is the University which can make delegated legislation in the form of Statutes or Ordinances).
holding: The interim order of this Court dated 22nd September, 2006, prima facie, amounts to judicial legislation and the question before us is whether this is legally permissible.
I am prima facie of the opinion that it is not.
